messages.subject: Re: STIFF ODE solver in STAN
parts:
Hi, Thierry.  I’m cc-ing Bob Carpenter and Daniel Lee, who are implementing the ODE solvers, and also cc-ing the stan-users list since others should be interested in this.  The short answer is that I think you should try the Stan ode solver (which we are planning to introduce in a near-future Stan version).  It’s hard for me to say ahead of time how well it will work on a particular example, but I will say that it will typically run better if the starting points are chosen carefully.
Andrew

Dear Professor Gelman,
 
I’m currently doing a PhD in pharmacometrics at the University of Manchester (UK) in collaboration with Novartis in Basel (Switzerland).
 
As part of my PhD project, I’m working on the application of physiologically-based pharmacokinetic models to clinical data using a Bayesian approach (three-stage hierarchical model with preclinical data as prior information).
I’d like for that to use Stan given the positive experience of my colleague Sebastian Weber with a PK-PD model defined with ODEs.
I can see that the next version of Stan will be released soon and will include a non-stiff ODE solver (based on the C++ “odeint” library if I’m right).
 
I’m sure you are familiar with PBPK systems which often are defined with stiff ODEs.
Therefore, do you think the solver implemented in the next Stan version would be adequate for such analysis? If not, does the team plan to  implement a solver for both non-stiff and stiff equations such as LSODA? If not, would you have any suggestion on which software/platform I could use to perform such Bayesian analysis?
 
Many thanks in advance for your help.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: STIFF ODE solver in STAN
parts:
Yes, we eventually plan to implement stiff solvers in Stan.
It might be a while, though, as in six to twelve months.

Do you know how LSODA deals with stiffness? That is, does
it calculate a Jacobian, and if so, how?

Depending on what your model is, you could use MCSim, written
by Frederic Bois, who's also helping us with Stan's ODE solvers.
I don't know if it'll support the kind of model you want, but
it looks pretty flexible.

- Bob

messages.author: 5a7d96b840c23bef
messages.subject: Re: STIFF ODE solver in STAN
parts:
Hi Thierry,

Like you, I am looking forward to implementation of ODE solvers in Stan. I plan to take advantage of them to construct Stan functions for PKPD modeling that can handle complicated event histories in a manner similar to NONMEM's NMTRAN and PREDPP components. A stiff ODE solver, or even better a solver that automatically adapts between solvers for non-stiff and stiff ODE's like LSODA, would be great. 

Until then one option is the BUGSModelLibrary package (https://code.google.com/p/bugsmodellibrary/) for WinBUGS 1.4.3. It gives the user a choice between multiple solvers including LSODA. The tradeoffs will be (possibly) more efficient ODE solving but less efficient sampling with WinBUGS/BUGSModelLibrary versus Stan with the non-stiff solver. It might be worth trying both options and selecting the one that performs best for your particular problem.

Regards,
Bill

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: STIFF ODE solver in STAN
parts:
A 200-fold difference could mean a slowdown of 200-fold.
It has to take a step size controlled by the fastest moving
variable.

How many parameters do you have there?

In Stan, the dimension of the solver (i.e., integrator) used is

N = (1 + num_params) * state_dimension

because we add to the original state y, the sensitivities d.state/d.param,
which is is a um_params * state_dimension matrix.

We need d.state/d.param in order to compute derivatives of
the solutions w.r.t. the parameters in order to use HMC.

For stiff systems, we then need to compute an N*N Jacobian.
So the slowdown's essentially going to be a constant * N-fold,
where the constant is the extra cost to evaluate with reverse-mode
nested in forward-mode autodiff compared to with just reverse-mode;
so maybe another factor of 2--4.

We're working on a new autodiff implementation that'll be much more
efficient at Hessians and Jacobians (and third-order calculations).

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: STIFF ODE solver in STAN
parts:
Our case is a bit special because we need the sensitivities
(derivatives of state w.r.t. parameters and initial state)
calculated along with the basic system solution. This
coupled system has a lot of structure, as Michael Betancourt's
been exploring. It turns out the Jacobian of the coupled
system is going to have a great deal of structure we can
exploit.

Systems like LSODA take the system as a whole, figure
out the Jacobians with finite diffs when they need to,
and try to do something clever with sparseness. You can
also plug in your own Jacobian function, which is what I
think we'll have to do in the end (though we'll probably try
just letting their built-ins loose and see how they do).
LSODA itself allows for banded Jacobians, which may turn out to
be sufficient to control the kinds of stiffness we care about.

For Stan 2.5, it'll just be Boost's Runge-Kutta implementation
for non-stiff system.

Hopefully in the next six to nine months we'll be able to
roll out something more robust to stiffness that's not too
onerous computationally.

And thanks to everyone for all the input --- we really appreciate
it!

- Bob
